methods.name: Stage-Progression
methods.rationale: Applies typical Series A → next-stage step-up multiplier (2.0x) to $25M total raised proxy.

methods.name: Peer-Median
methods.skip_reason: insufficient narrow peer set in Chips & Semiconductors (found 1 same-stage, 1 adjacent-stage, 0 similar-tier; need ≥3)
methods.rationale: 12 same-sector peers exist in Chips & Semiconductors, but none of the narrow filters (same-stage / adjacent-stage / similar-valuation-tier) yielded ≥3 datapoints. Falling back to all-sector median would be misleading.

data.narrative:
Finwave Semiconductor is a Series A–stage chip design company founded by Tomas Palacios and Bin Lu, operating in a competitive landscape of 12 same-sector peers (3 public: ALAB, NVDA, AMD; 8 private including SambaNova, Cerebras, and Credo).

Stage-progression analysis represents the sole applicable valuation method. Using the company's $25M+ total capital raised as a proxy for current value and applying a 2.0x multiplier typical of Series A–to–subsequent–stage advancement yields an implied valuation of $50M. This methodology is straightforward but relies on the assumption that the capital-raised figure accurately reflects investor consensus at the most recent round. Peer-median analysis could not be applied due to insufficient narrow-set comparables; while the semiconductor sector includes sufficient breadth, filtering to same-stage or adjacent-stage peers yielded fewer than three datapoints. Public-comp anchoring using the three public semiconductors' median price-to-sales multiple of 21.0x is inapplicable absent Finwave's disclosed revenue.

The analysis supports a valuation range of $42M to $57M, centered on $50M. This narrow range reflects reliance on a single triangulation method and should be weighted accordingly. Key uncertainties include the true representativeness of the $25M raised figure as a valuation proxy, the applicability of standard stage-step multipliers to frontier semiconductor ventures, and the absence of revenue visibility necessary for comparative public-market anchoring.
